messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Thoeun

Thoeun was sixty-eight when his partner of seventeen years struck him for the first time. It happened on an ordinary Tuesday evening in their Arlington apartment, the kind of moment that should have been unremarkable—Thoeun had come home late from his job as a nanny, tired from managing four young children all day. His partner, whom he had trusted completely, had been drinking. An argument about money escalated quickly into something Thoeun had never anticipated. The blow came from behind, a heavy object—he would never be entirely certain what—and then his partner's fists, methodical and sustained, while Thoeun found himself on the floor, his body curled defensively, his arms raised but ineffective. He had frozen rather than fought back. The terror of it was not the pain, though there was considerable pain; it was the absolute helplessness, the sense that he had become a thing to be broken rather than a person. The violence lasted perhaps five minutes, though time had collapsed entirely. When it stopped, Thoeun lay still, afraid that movement would provoke more.

That was four years ago. In the years since, Thoeun had remained in the relationship—he had nowhere else to go, no family in the country, and he had come to believe that the violence was somehow his fault, that he had provoked it through his own inadequacy. The physical injuries healed, but something deeper did not. When memories of that night surfaced—and they did, unbidden, often while he was doing something ordinary like washing dishes or sitting with the children he cared for—the terror returned with it, undiminished by time. His body would tense as if bracing for impact again, his arms would draw inward, and he would feel himself back on that floor, helpless and small. The memory itself felt strange to him, almost as though it belonged to someone else's life rather than his own, something he had witnessed rather than endured. Yet when it came, the fear was entirely his own.

Over these four years, Thoeun had developed careful strategies for keeping the terror at bay. He had learned never to allow anger to surface—anger, he believed, was dangerous, something that would make him a target. He kept it buried so thoroughly that he sometimes wondered if he still felt it at all. He avoided being in the dark, keeping lights on throughout the apartment even when his partner was sleeping, because darkness had become synonymous with vulnerability. He avoided anything that might be stressful: difficult conversations with his employer, social gatherings, even the small conflicts that arise naturally in any job. At work, with the children, he had become almost preternaturally calm, almost absent in a way that some parents had begun to notice.

The hypervigilance had become his constant companion. Unexpected movements—a child darting around a corner, his partner shifting in bed at night—would send a spike of pure alarm through his nervous system, his body reacting as though danger were imminent. Even in moments when he knew logically that he was safe, even sitting in the bright morning sunlight with the children laughing around him, his shoulders remained tense, his breathing shallow. He could not remember what it felt like to truly relax. The startle responses had become so frequent that one of the families he worked for had gently suggested that perhaps he was overworked, that he seemed "on edge."

What frightened Thoeun most was that the more he tried to suppress his feelings and avoid anything that might trigger the memories, the more the memories seemed to push through. When he succeeded in keeping anger locked away, the recalled terror would arrive instead, his body remembering what his mind tried to forget. And when the memory came, with all its sensory immediacy and the overwhelming helplessness of it, he would find himself reaching for avoidance again—turning away from his partner, making excuses to work late, staying in the brightly lit kitchen rather than going to bed. The cycle had tightened over months until Thoeun felt trapped in a narrowing corridor, each escape route closing behind him. It was only when his employer expressed concern that he might need to take medical leave, that his hands had begun to shake too visibly while feeding the toddlers, that Thoeun finally admitted to his primary care physician what had happened. At seventy-two, he had come to understand that he could not manage this alone any longer. What he needed most was to believe that he could survive without the constant vigilance, without the suppression, without the terror—but he had no idea how that might be possible.
